data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a pragmatic, non-inductive rule of action based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), where the cost is accepting that we can never know if our theories are true, only that they are closer to the truth than their falsified rivals.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If the formal definition of verisimilitude remains logically incoherent for comparing false theories, rendering the metric unusable.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If acting on a theory necessarily implies an assumption of its future reliability, which is an inductive leap regardless of the label 'verisimilitude'.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "Popper replaces the inductive goal of 'probability' with the comparative metric of 'verisimilitude'. A theory with higher corroboration has survived more severe tests, implying it has greater truth-content and/or less falsity-content than a rival. The preference is rational not because the theory is likely true, but because it is the best available approximation of truth. This avoids induction by refusing to assign a probability value to the theory itself. This is precisely the result Erdos and Renyi established in their 1959 paper, which states this conclusion in exactly these terms.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": []}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
